title: THEY MARKED A DAY FOR THEIR DEATH. GOD TURNED IT INTO A DAY THEY WOULD NEVER FORGET.
paragraphs: THEY MARKED A DAY FOR THEIR DEATH. GOD TURNED IT INTO A DAY THEY WOULD NEVER FORGET.

Why Did the Jews Establish the Feast of Purim? — Esther 9:20–28 | The terrifying story of a death sentence, a hidden deliverance, and the God who can turn the day meant to destroy you into a testimony of His faithfulness.
There was a date on the calendar when an entire people were supposed to die.
Not just the soldiers. Not just the leaders. Not just the people who had offended someone powerful.
The children, too.
The mothers holding their babies. The fathers trying to protect their families. The elderly who had survived wars, exile, and years of uncertainty.
All of them.
One day had been chosen for their destruction.
And somewhere in the Persian Empire, ordinary Jewish families were living with the knowledge that their enemies had been given legal permission to kill them.
Imagine trying to sleep with that knowledge.
Imagine looking at your children and wondering whether you would still be alive to hold them when that day arrived.
Imagine praying while the calendar kept moving.
One day closer.
Another day closer.
And heaven seemed silent.
But here is what makes the story of Purim so unforgettable.
The date that was chosen for their destruction became the date their descendants would celebrate their deliverance.
The very thing intended to erase their future became part of the story their children would remember.
And before you dismiss this as an ancient Jewish festival with little connection to your life, consider something.
Have you ever lived through a season when the future frightened you more than the present?
When something beyond your control threatened everything you loved?
When you prayed, but nothing seemed to change?
When God seemed absent, and you wondered whether He was doing anything at all?
Then you may understand more of Esther's story than you realize.
Because Purim is not merely about people surviving a crisis.
It is about remembering a deliverance so extraordinary that forgetting it would have been another tragedy.
And for Christians reading Esther in the light of the whole Bible, it also invites us to look toward the greater redemption accomplished through Jesus Christ.
But to understand why the Jews established Purim, we must first understand the terror that made the celebration necessary.
The story begins with a man named Haman.
Haman was not an ordinary enemy.

He held tremendous authority under King Ahasuerus, commonly identified with Xerxes I of Persia. He possessed political influence, royal access, and enough personal pride to turn one man's refusal to honor him into a campaign against an entire people.
That man was Mordecai, a Jew living in the Persian Empire.
When Mordecai refused to bow down to Haman, Haman's anger grew beyond personal revenge.
Esther 3:6 explains that Haman sought to destroy all the Jews throughout the kingdom.
Think about the terrifying disproportion.
One man's wounded pride.
An entire people's threatened extinction.
Haman then cast lots to determine the date of his planned destruction.
Esther 3:7 records that the lot was cast in the first month, Nisan, and that the selected date fell in the twelfth month, Adar.
The Hebrew word for the lot is פּוּר — pur.
It refers to a lot used to make a selection or determine an outcome.
This small Hebrew word matters because it eventually becomes the name of the entire celebration.
But at first, it represented something horrifying.
A date selected for death.
Haman obtained royal authorization for a decree permitting the destruction of the Jews on the thirteenth day of Adar.
Esther 3:13 describes the order to destroy, kill, and annihilate the Jews, including young and old, women and children, and to plunder their possessions.
This was not a misunderstanding.
This was not an ordinary disagreement.
It was an empire-wide threat of mass violence.
And the Jews could not simply pretend it would disappear.
The decree bore the authority of the Persian king.
The date was set.
The machinery of destruction had begun moving.
Then something happened that makes Esther one of the most remarkable books in Scripture.
A Jewish woman was already inside the palace.
Her name was Esther.
She had become queen, but her Jewish identity had not initially been disclosed to the king.
Mordecai urged her to intervene.
Yet approaching the king without being summoned could cost her life.
Esther was facing a decision that would expose the difference between possessing influence and being willing to risk it.
Would she remain silent?
Would she protect her position?
Or would she identify herself with a threatened people and accept the danger?
Mordecai confronted her with a question that has echoed through generations.
In Esther 4:14, he asked whether she had come to her royal position for such a time as this.
Notice something important.
Mordecai did not claim to know every detail of God's hidden purposes.
He expressed confidence that deliverance could arise from another place, while warning Esther that her own position would not guarantee her safety.
Esther responded by calling for a fast.
Then she made her decision.
She would approach the king.
And if she perished, she perished.
There is something profoundly moving about that moment.
Courage did not mean Esther had received a guarantee that nothing painful could happen.
Courage meant she would do what was necessary even when the outcome remained uncertain.
Some of the most significant acts of faithfulness happen when people have no certainty of earthly safety.
A mother keeps praying.
A father chooses integrity.
A wounded believer refuses to repay evil with evil.
Someone finally tells the truth.
Someone stands beside the vulnerable, knowing there may be consequences.
Not every courageous decision ends with an earthly rescue.
The Bible never promises that it will.
But Esther reminds us that fear does not have to make the final decision.
And then the story begins to turn.
Haman prepares a structure on which he intends to have Mordecai executed.
But the king experiences a sleepless night.
The royal chronicles are read aloud.
A previously overlooked act of loyalty by Mordecai is brought to the king's attention.
Haman arrives expecting to advance his own plans, only to be instructed to honor the very man he hates.
Eventually, Esther exposes Haman's plot before the king.
The man who sought Mordecai's death is executed on the structure he had prepared for Mordecai.
The reversal is astonishing.
But the danger is not over.
The original royal decree remains a threat.
According to Esther 8, another decree is issued, authorizing the Jews to assemble and defend themselves against those who attack them.
When the appointed day arrives, the Jews prevail over their enemies.

The biblical account does not present this as a harmless celebration or a conflict without bloodshed. Esther 9 records deaths and violent confrontation, and those difficult details must not be erased.
It also repeatedly states that the Jews did not lay hands on the plunder, even though the royal authorization had permitted them to take it.
The account distinguishes their defense against hostile attackers from a campaign of enrichment.
By the time the conflict ends, the people who had expected destruction have experienced deliverance.
Their mourning is turned into gladness.
Their fear gives way to relief.
Their threatened future becomes a future they can pass on to their children.
And this is where Esther 9:20–28 answers the question at the heart of the story.
Why did the Jews establish the Feast of Purim?
Because they refused to let the memory of their deliverance disappear.
Mordecai wrote to the Jews throughout the provinces of the Persian Empire, instructing them to observe the fourteenth and fifteenth days of Adar annually.
Esther 9:22 describes those days in the King James Version as the time when the Jews rested from their enemies, and the month that had been turned:
“from sorrow to joy, and from mourning into a good day.”
The Hebrew text makes the reversal especially vivid.
מִיָּגוֹן לְשִׂמְחָה וּמֵאֵבֶל לְיוֹם טוֹב
Mi-yagon le-simchah, u-me'evel le-yom tov.
Literally, the expression conveys the movement from grief to joy, and from mourning to a good or festive day.
The Hebrew word yagon means grief or sorrow.
Simchah means joy or gladness.
Evel refers to mourning.
And yom tov means a good day, here describing a festive occasion.
These words are not decorative poetry placed over a pleasant memory.
They describe a complete reversal of the people's circumstances.
The Jews had expected to mourn their dead.
Instead, they were able to celebrate their survival.
They had faced a decree intended to destroy their families.
Instead, they could gather with those families and remember their deliverance.
What had been a month of dread became a month of joy.
And they wanted future generations to know why.
Esther 9:26 explains the festival's name:
“Wherefore they called these days Purim after the name of Pur.”
Purim is the plural form associated with pur, the lot Haman had cast.
Consider the extraordinary irony.
The festival was named after the very instrument Haman had used to select the day of their destruction.
Every time the people spoke the name Purim, they recalled the threat from which they had been delivered.
The name did not hide the darkness of the story.
It remembered that the darkness had not prevailed.
This is one reason Purim has such enduring significance in Jewish life.
It preserves the memory of a people who survived an existential threat, and it celebrates the reversal described in the book of Esther.
But there is another detail many readers overlook.
The celebration was never intended to remain a private feeling.
Esther 9:22 describes feasting, gladness, sending portions of food to one another, and giving gifts to the poor.
Joy was meant to move outward.
Those who had survived together were to celebrate together.
Those with food were to share.
Those who were poor were not to be forgotten.
The people were not simply told to remember what happened.
They were given practices that would carry that remembrance into their communities.
And this confronts something in us.
Sometimes we become so consumed with our own relief that we forget the person who is still suffering.
We thank God for provision but fail to notice the hungry.
We celebrate answered prayers but forget those who are still waiting.
We rejoice that our families are safe while remaining indifferent to families living in fear.
Purim reminds its observers that communal deliverance calls for communal remembrance and generosity.
And Christians can recognize a wider biblical principle here: gratitude should make us more generous, not less.
The God we thank with our lips must not be dishonored by the way we treat our neighbors.
But perhaps the most haunting feature of Esther is something the book never directly says.
In the Hebrew text of Esther, the name of God is not explicitly mentioned.
Not once.
That does not mean the story teaches that God was absent.
It means the book tells its story without an explicit declaration identifying God's action at every turn.
Readers are invited to notice the remarkable convergence of events.
Esther becomes queen.
Mordecai uncovers a plot against the king.
His loyalty is recorded but initially unrewarded.
The king cannot sleep at a decisive moment.
The chronicles are read.
Mordecai's earlier act is discovered.
Haman's plans collapse.
The Jews survive.
The narrative never gives us permission to claim that we can identify God's purpose behind every painful event in our own lives.

Yet its pattern has long led Jewish and Christian readers to reflect on providence: the possibility of divine care operating through circumstances that appear ordinary, uncertain, or even threatening.
And that speaks to the person reading this who has been quietly asking:
Where is God?
Where was He when the diagnosis came?
Where was He when the marriage fell apart?
Where was He when the person you trusted betrayed you?
Where was He when you prayed until you had no more words?
Those questions deserve more than a shallow religious slogan.
Esther does not explain every mystery of suffering.
It does not promise that every believer will escape tragedy.
And it does not teach that every painful chapter will end with the kind of public reversal Esther experienced.
But it challenges the assumption that God's silence in our perception proves His absence.
Sometimes we do not understand what is happening.
Sometimes we cannot see the outcome.
Sometimes obedience must continue without an explanation.
And sometimes the evidence of God's faithfulness becomes clearer only when we look backward.
That is part of why remembrance matters.
Because suffering can distort our perspective.
Fear can make yesterday's mercy feel distant.
Grief can make us forget what once sustained us.
And even after deliverance, human beings are remarkably capable of forgetting.
The Jews established Purim so that the story would not be swallowed by time.
Esther 9:28 declares that these days were to be remembered and kept throughout generations, families, provinces, and cities.
The text specifically emphasizes that the remembrance of Purim should not perish among their descendants.
This was more than a holiday.
It was an intentional act of historical memory.
Parents would tell children.
Communities would gather.
The story would be read.
The threatened destruction and the extraordinary reversal would remain part of the people's identity.
They would remember that their survival had once been in danger.
And they would remember that the danger had not been the end of their story.
Now we must ask an important question.
What does any of this have to do with Jesus Christ?
To answer faithfully, we must first honor what Esther actually says.
Purim is a Jewish festival, not a Christian ordinance.
Esther 9 does not command Christians to observe Purim, nor does it explicitly identify Esther, Mordecai, or the festival as direct prophecies of Jesus.
We should not force Christ's name into verses where the biblical author did not place it.
Yet Christians read the Old Testament as part of the larger biblical story that finds its fulfillment in Christ.
And within that larger story, the preservation of the Jewish people matters profoundly.
God's promises to Abraham included blessing for the nations through his offspring (Genesis 12:3; 22:18).
The Messiah would come through Israel.
The New Testament identifies Jesus as the son of David, the son of Abraham (Matthew 1:1), and Paul writes that Christ came from Israel according to His human ancestry (Romans 9:5).
The preservation celebrated in Esther belongs within that history of God's covenant dealings with Israel.
But the connection becomes even more powerful when we consider the biblical theme of reversal.
At Purim, a day intended for destruction became a time of deliverance.
At the cross, Jesus willingly entered the suffering and death that human sin and evil brought upon Him.
The rulers who crucified Him believed they had brought His mission to an end.
His followers watched Him die.
His body was placed in a tomb.
And for a moment, hope appeared buried.
But the resurrection revealed that death had not defeated Him.
Acts 2:23–24 declares that Jesus was delivered up according to God's definite plan and foreknowledge, crucified by lawless men, and raised by God.
Human wickedness was real.
Christ's suffering was real.
His death was real.
And His resurrection was real.
The cross was not merely an unfortunate event that God later repaired.
According to Scripture, Jesus gave Himself for our sins in accordance with God's saving purpose (Galatians 1:4).
Here we encounter something greater than a reversal of earthly danger.
Through Jesus Christ, sinners are offered forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life.
The threatened Jews in Esther needed deliverance from those who sought to kill them.
Every human being also faces a deeper spiritual problem: sin and separation from a holy God.
Romans 3:23 says that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
Romans 6:23 declares that the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
And Romans 5:8 announces the astonishing heart of the Gospel:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
That is grace.
Not God pretending our sin does not matter.
Not God calling evil good.
Not God offering cheap reassurance without repentance.
Grace is God giving His Son to save people who could never save themselves.
Jesus did not come merely to make difficult lives more comfortable.
He came to save sinners.
He died for our sins.
He rose from the dead.
And He calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
That is why the Christian hope is deeper than the promise that every frightening situation will disappear.
Even when earthly circumstances do not change as we desire, the risen Christ remains the believer's hope.
Even when death comes, it does not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
Even when a life has been scarred by sin, forgiveness and transformation are possible through His grace.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this needs to hear.
You may have spent years believing your worst chapter defines you.
The affair.
The addiction.
The secret.
The betrayal.
The years of pretending.
The faith you abandoned.
The family you hurt.
The prayers you stopped praying because you were ashamed to face God.
You remember things other people know nothing about.
You know how to smile while carrying guilt.
You know how to sit through worship while feeling spiritually distant.
You know how to tell people you are fine when your conscience is exhausted.
And somewhere along the way, you may have begun to believe that your story is already decided.
But hear the Gospel clearly.
Your sin is serious. Your shame is not your savior. And your past is not more powerful than the grace of Jesus Christ.
You cannot rewrite history.
You cannot undo every consequence.
You cannot force broken relationships to heal on your timetable.
But you can come to Christ in repentance and faith.
You can confess what you have hidden.
You can turn away from the sin you have defended.
You can receive the forgiveness that Jesus purchased through His death and resurrection.
First John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
That promise is not an invitation to continue in sin without concern.
It is an invitation to stop hiding and come into the light.
The Gospel does not promise that repentance will erase every earthly consequence.
It promises something infinitely precious: forgiveness and reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
And that is where the theme of this ministry becomes more than a memorable phrase.
Not because Jesus changes the facts of what happened.
Not because He makes every painful memory vanish.
Not because the damage caused by sin suddenly becomes insignificant.
But because He can redeem sinners, transform lives, and give an eternal future that human failure could never produce.
The apostle Paul once persecuted the church.
Peter denied knowing Jesus.
The thief beside Christ had no lifetime left to rebuild his reputation.
Yet the New Testament bears witness to the mercy of God reaching people in profoundly different circumstances.
No sinner should presume upon grace.
And no repentant sinner should conclude that Christ is unwilling to receive those who truly come to Him.
Jesus Himself declared in John 6:37 that whoever comes to Him He will never cast out.
Think about that.
You may have been rejected by people.
You may have destroyed your own reputation.
You may have reached a point where you struggle to believe you could ever change.
But Jesus calls sinners to Himself.
Not to remain enslaved to sin.
Not to celebrate rebellion.
But to be forgiven, reconciled, and transformed.
The story of Purim begins with a people facing a day of destruction.
It ends with a people establishing days of remembrance.
The Christian Gospel tells of a Savior who entered death and rose victorious, opening the way to eternal life for all who trust in Him.
These are distinct biblical events, and we should never confuse them.
Yet both remind us that apparent finality is not always the final word.
And for the believer, the resurrection of Jesus is the decisive reason for hope.
Maybe you are still in the middle of a chapter you do not understand.
Maybe you are praying for a child who has walked away from faith.
Maybe your family is carrying a burden nobody else sees.
Maybe you are trying to rebuild trust after years of failure.
Maybe you are grieving someone you desperately wish you could speak to again.
I will not tell you that every earthly loss will be reversed.
I will not promise that tomorrow will bring the answer you want.
But I will tell you what Scripture allows us to say with confidence.
Jesus Christ is risen.
His grace is sufficient for those who belong to Him.
His call to repentance is still open.
And nothing can separate those who are in Christ from the love of God in Him (Romans 8:38–39).
So do not confuse an unfinished chapter with an abandoned life.
Do not confuse unanswered questions with proof that God does not care.
And do not let shame convince you to run away from the only Savior who can forgive you.
Come to Jesus.
Not after you have repaired yourself.
Not after you have made your life look respectable.
Come with repentance.
Come with faith.
Come with the truth.
Because the One who died and rose again is not asking you to manufacture your own redemption.
He calls you to receive the salvation He alone can give.
And if this article has exposed something you have been hiding, I want to invite you to respond—not for appearance, not for applause, but with sincerity.
If you are exhausted from struggling, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.”
You do not have to disclose private wounds or painful details publicly. A few honest words are enough to let fellow believers know you desire prayer.
Someone who is still waiting may need the encouragement of hearing how Christ has sustained you.
Before you leave, remember something else from Purim.
The people did not keep their deliverance to themselves.
They passed the memory forward.
They made sure the next generation would know.
And today, you have an opportunity to pass biblical truth forward, too.
There is also a practical way to help this work continue.
Gospel Warrior exists to make biblical truth accessible, to encourage believers toward deeper discipleship, and to keep pointing people to Jesus Christ.
Keeping these resources available, developing new teaching materials, and expanding the reach of this ministry require time, labor, and financial support.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
You can glorify Him through obedience, worship, generosity, service, prayer, and faithful love for others.
And whether or not you are able to give financially, your prayers, thoughtful comments, and willingness to share sound biblical teaching are genuinely valuable.
A simple Facebook share can introduce someone to a passage of Scripture they have never considered.
A personal invitation can encourage a discouraged believer to begin reading the Bible again.
A prayer can strengthen someone whose struggle you may never fully know.
And a faithful testimony can point attention away from human achievement and toward the mercy of Christ.
That is worth remembering.
Because Purim was established so that the generations after Esther would not forget the deliverance their ancestors had experienced.
And Christians, above all, have been entrusted with a message that must never be forgotten.
Christ died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day.
And forgiveness and eternal life are proclaimed in His name.
This is not merely a story about surviving a difficult season.
It is an invitation to remember who God is, to take sin seriously, to trust the risen Savior, and to live in the light of His grace.
The Jews called their celebration Purim because of the lot that had once marked their threatened destruction.
What Haman intended to be remembered as a day of terror became a yearly remembrance of deliverance.
And if you belong to Jesus Christ, your deepest hope does not rest on whether every earthly circumstance turns out the way you desire.
It rests on the Savior who conquered death.
So when you remember Esther, remember the courage.
Remember the threatened people.
Remember the reversal.
Remember the generations who were taught not to forget.
And when you look toward the cross and the empty tomb, remember something greater still.
The Savior who bore our sins is alive.
The door of repentance is open.
The invitation of grace is real.
And the story of every person who comes to Christ is forever changed by Him.
The day you thought your story was over may become the day you finally discover that Jesus, not your past, has the final word.
